title: 27. Live Coding / Take-Home
description: Turing S3 (60 min live) + Turing take-home (5-hr project + Loom walkthrough) + Andela pair-programming (60 min). Includes the actual patterns candidates report: editor-clone, refactor dirty 500-line codebase, stateful simulation (door-handler archetype), reasoning-box writeup, file I/O + threads. Each drill has real time budget.

27.1 Refactor Dirty Codebase: Small commits — never one big rewrite
27.2 Turing Live-Coding Warm-ups: Explicit complexity + edge cases at end
27.3 Stateful Simulation (Andela): Write step-by-step trace as you code
27.4 Take-Home + Loom Defense: 5-hour scope — plan the cut before coding
Loom: 15 min max, explain architecture + one thing you'd change
27.6 File I/O + Threading Kata (Andela): Never blocking event loop with sync I/O

questions.prompt: 35-min drill: given this 500-line Express handler doing parse + validate + persist + email + Kafka + audit + response, refactor toward SOLID without breaking tests. Talk through your first 3 minutes before you touch code.

rubric.criterion: Reads top-to-bottom first, names responsibilities
Adds characterization tests BEFORE refactor
Proposes: controller (thin) → service → repository → notifier/publisher
Uses DI for external services (SES, Kafka)
Handles txn boundary + outbox for email + Kafka
Pragmatic split — not 20 files for one handler

questions.modelAnswer: First 3 min: read every line, note responsibilities in comments — 'here it parses', 'here it charges', 'here it emails'. Before touching: write 2-3 characterization tests locking current behavior. Then split: OrderController (10 lines HTTP), OrderService (business logic), OrderRepository (DB), Notifier interface. Wrap email + Kafka in outbox pattern in same txn. Test each after extraction. Ship in 3 commits, not 1.

questions.prompt: You inherit a 400-line React component. 35-min drill: refactor toward hooks + subcomponents without breaking behavior.

rubric.criterion: Lock behavior with React Testing Library tests first
Extract data-fetching into useX hook
Extract form state into useReducer or react-hook-form
Split JSX into subcomponents by visual section
Memoize only after measuring
Commit in small reviewable chunks

questions.modelAnswer: Order: (1) capture behavior in RTL tests (user-facing assertions), (2) pull data-fetching + caching into useX hook, (3) form state → useReducer / react-hook-form, (4) split JSX by visual section into subcomponents, (5) profile with React DevTools BEFORE adding memoization, (6) each step = own commit + PR-sized chunk.

questions.prompt: 3000-line file, no tests, must add a new feature in 2 weeks. Walk through approach.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't propose rewrite up front
Adds characterization tests around affected paths BEFORE code
Introduces seam (Michael Feathers) at change point
Strangler-fig: new feature in isolated module, called from legacy
Ships in small PRs, each green in CI

questions.modelAnswer: Read the file, take notes on responsibilities. Write characterization tests (assert current behavior, warts and all) around 2 functions the feature touches. Introduce a seam — pass new dependency as parameter. Build new module in isolation, unit-test fully, wire in behind feature flag. Ship. Cleanup later.

questions.prompt: Convert this callback-heavy Node module to async/await while preserving error semantics. 30 min.

rubric.criterion: util.promisify for existing callback APIs
Preserves error propagation — no swallowed rejects
Handles parallel vs sequential decisions explicitly
Adds tests before + after

questions.modelAnswer: Use `util.promisify` on existing (err, res) callbacks. Convert one function at a time, run tests. Where callbacks were fired in parallel (via async.parallel or manual counter), use `Promise.all`. Where sequential, use `for-await`. Every catch either handles or rethrows — never swallows. Add tests locking behavior before refactoring each.

questions.prompt: Refactor a 'God class' (UserService with 40 methods handling auth, profile, billing, notifications) into cohesive units.

rubric.criterion: Names Single Responsibility violation
Splits by domain: AuthService, ProfileService, BillingService, NotificationService
Preserves public API via facade if callers can't be updated
Introduces DI for cross-service deps
Test coverage improves as extraction progresses

questions.modelAnswer: Split by domain. AuthService (login/logout/reset), ProfileService (get/update), BillingService (charge/refund), NotificationService (email/SMS). Keep UserService as a facade forwarding to the new services if callers can't be updated in one PR. DI cross-deps. As each is extracted, add unit tests specific to that service. Delete the facade last.

questions.prompt: 60 min: build a VSCode-like text editor from scratch. Design + implement together. Insert / delete / cursor movement / undo. Narrate every decision.
30 min: Tic-Tac-Toe in Node REPL. Two-player, prints board, detects winner + tie.
25 min: parse a raw stack trace, dedupe consecutive identical frames, output cleaned version.
30 min: parse Nginx access log lines, count top 10 IPs by request volume.
25 min: dedupe a CSV by 'email' column, keep the row with the latest 'updated_at'.
30 min: in-memory token-bucket rate limiter, per-key, N tokens refilling at R/sec.
30 min: URL shortener core (in-memory). shorten(url) → 6-char code; resolve(code) → url. Handle collisions.
30 min: deep diff of two JSON objects. Return { added, removed, changed } keyed by path.
30 min: in-memory pub/sub. subscribe(topic, fn) → id; unsubscribe(id); publish(topic, msg) fires all subs.
30 min: LRU Cache — get(k) and put(k,v) both O(1). Warm-up favorite at Turing/Anthropic.
50 min (Andela signature): Door state machine. States: closed / opening / open / closing. Events: press-button (toggles), obstacle-detected (reverses), pause / resume. Print each transition.
50 min: elevator simulator. Handle requests from N floors, direction preference, capacity limit, emergency stop.
40 min: vending machine. Insert coins, select item, dispense change. Handle out-of-stock + insufficient funds.
50 min: ATM simulator. Login (PIN with 3-attempt lockout), balance, withdraw (multiple of 20, sufficient funds, daily limit).
40 min: traffic light controller for a 4-way intersection. Configurable timing. Emergency preempt (turn all red, allow pass).
Take-home: build a mini-app using the client's public API. 5 hours. Submit code + 15-min Loom walkthrough. How do you plan?

rubric.criterion: Plans the CUT before coding (first 30 min)
Aims for shippable-narrow, not sprawling
README explains: setup, run, tradeoffs made, what you'd add next
1-2 tests per module — not full coverage
Commit history tells the story (many small commits > one big)
Loom: 15 min max, architecture + one thing you'd change

questions.modelAnswer: First 30 min: read the API docs, decide on 1 primary user story + 2 stretch. Sketch data flow on paper. Choose stack you'll type fastest in (not most impressive). Hours 1-3: build the primary story end-to-end (backend + frontend + one integration test). Hour 4: add ONE polish item (auth, error handling, or a nice UI touch). Hour 5: write README (setup + tradeoffs + 'if I had 5 more hours I'd…'). Record Loom: walk architecture (2 min), demo happy path (5 min), show one interesting decision (5 min), name one thing I'd redo (3 min). Push commits along the way — not one squash.

questions.prompt: Write your 15-min Loom script structure. What do you cover, in what order?

rubric.criterion: Opens with 60-sec context: what the ask was, what you shipped
Architecture walk (2-3 min) with a diagram
Live demo of happy path (3-5 min)
Deep-dive one interesting decision (3-5 min) — trade-off shown
Explicit 'what I'd change with more time' (2 min)
Doesn't overrun 15 min

questions.modelAnswer: 0:00-1:00 Context: 'The ask was X. I chose to focus on Y because Z. In 5 hours I shipped A, B, C.' 1:00-3:30 Architecture: show README diagram + 5 key files. 3:30-8:00 Demo happy path end-to-end. 8:00-12:00 Deep-dive: 'One decision I want to highlight is how I handled X. I chose approach Y over Z because [tradeoff]. Downside is [honest cost]. Here's the code.' 12:00-14:00 'If I had 5 more hours I'd (1) add pagination, (2) refactor Y into…, (3) write integration tests for Z.' 14:00-15:00 Wrap: 'Thanks, happy to defend any decision on the follow-up call.'

questions.prompt: Write the README structure for a take-home submission. What sections + what goes in each?

rubric.criterion: Setup / run instructions that work from a fresh clone
What was built + what wasn't (scope honesty)
Tradeoffs section — decisions + why
'If I had more time' section
How to run tests
Architecture diagram (ascii or image)

questions.prompt: Interviewer challenges: 'Why didn't you use TypeScript? Why did you skip auth? Why is your test coverage so low?' Defend live.

rubric.criterion: Doesn't apologize; defends decisions with rationale
Names the trade explicitly ('I chose X because Y, cost was Z')
Acknowledges where they'd do differently at scale / with more time
Never says 'ran out of time' as sole excuse
Ends with concrete 'here's what I'd do next'

questions.modelAnswer: TS: 'I chose JS because I move faster in it and 5 hours is tight. For a prod project I'd start in TS — the refactor cost later is real.' Auth: 'I skipped it deliberately — the primary story you asked about is X, and auth would have taken 2 hours from that. I noted it as first thing to add.' Coverage: 'I wrote 2 integration tests covering the happy path + one edge case. Unit-testing every service would have doubled my time and given diminishing returns for a demo. For prod I'd want ~70% coverage focused on business logic.'

questions.prompt: What does a good commit history look like for a take-home?

rubric.criterion: Many small commits telling the build story
Each commit does ONE thing
Messages describe the WHY not just WHAT
No single 'wip' or 'final' squash

questions.modelAnswer: Bad: 1 commit 'submission'. Good: 8-12 commits showing progression. Example: 'scaffold Next.js', 'add User model with Prisma', 'implement /api/users POST with validation', 'add rate limit note in README', 'unit test User.create', 'add JWT auth (skipped in scope, marked TODO)', 'refactor service to inject db for testing', 'README with tradeoffs'. Reviewers can follow your thinking + see you didn't paste code from anywhere.

questions.prompt: Fill in the reasoning-box template for Two Sum. As if grading yourself for Andela Qualified.

rubric.criterion: Every section from the template filled
Approach + why hash-map over brute force / sort+two-pointer
Correct complexity
Actual edge cases named

questions.modelAnswer:
## Problem: Given nums[] and target, return indices of two nums adding to target. Exactly one solution exists.
## Assumptions: single valid pair; nums can be negative; length ≥ 2
## Approach: Hash-map value→index, single pass. On each element compute need = target - n; if need is in map, return [map[need], i]; else store n → i.
Alternatives: brute force O(n²) — too slow for large n; sort+two-pointer O(n log n) — loses original indices, would need extra work.
## Complexity: Time O(n), Space O(n).
## Edge cases: uses index i first (won't self-match), works for negatives, works when both nums equal (need != current until second iter).
## Tests I'd add: all negatives, target=0 with [-3,3], very large n for perf.
## Scale: 10x holds; hash lookup is amortized O(1).

questions.prompt: Fill the reasoning-box for Valid Parentheses. Include your own tradeoff analysis.

rubric.criterion: Full template filled
Approach: stack + pair-map
Complexity + edge cases

questions.modelAnswer:
## Problem: Return true if string of ()[]{}  is balanced.
## Assumptions: only these 6 chars; empty string is balanced (true).
## Approach: Stack of expected closers. On '(' push ')', on '[' push ']', on '{' push '}'. On any closer, pop and compare — if mismatch or stack empty, return false. End: return stack.length === 0.
Alt: pair-map + comparison on close — same complexity, personal style.
## Complexity: Time O(n), Space O(n) worst case.
## Edge cases: empty (true), only openers (false), only closers (false), mismatched pairs.
## Tests: '()[]{}' true, '(]' false, '' true, '(((' false, ')))' false.
## Scale: linear — holds fine.
